62:2.ar: هُوَ ٱلَّذِي بَعَثَ فِي ٱلۡأُمِّيِّـۧنَ رَسُولࣰ ا مِّنۡهُمۡ يَتۡلُواْ عَلَيۡهِمۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ وَيُزَكِّيهِمۡ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَٱلۡحِكۡمَةَ وَإِن كَانُواْ مِن قَبۡلُ لَفِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينࣲ‏
62:2.en: He it is Who hath sent among the unlettered ones a messenger of their own, to recite unto them His revelations and to make them grow, and to teach them the Scripture and wisdom, though heretofore they were indeed in error manifest

62:5.ar: مَثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ حُمِّلُواْ ٱلتَّوۡرَىٰةَ ثُمَّ لَمۡ يَحۡمِلُوهَا كَمَثَلِ ٱلۡحِمَارِ يَحۡمِلُ أَسۡفَارَۢاۚ بِئۡسَ مَثَلُ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلَّذِينَ كَذَّبُواْ بِـَٔايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِۚ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَهۡدِي ٱلۡقَوۡمَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
62:5.en: The likeness of those who are entrusted with the Law of Moses, yet apply it not, is as the likeness of the ass carrying books. Wretched is the likeness of folk who deny the revelations of Allah. And Allah guideth not wrongdoing folk

62:6.ar: قُلۡ يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ هَادُوٓاْ إِن زَعَمۡتُمۡ أَنَّكُمۡ أَوۡلِيَآءُ لِلَّهِ مِن دُونِ ٱلنَّاسِ فَتَمَنَّوُاْ ٱلۡمَوۡتَ إِن كُنتُمۡ صَٰدِقِينَ
62:6.en: Say (O Muhammad): O ye who are Jews! If ye claim that ye are favoured of Allah apart from (all) mankind, then long for death if ye are truthful

62:7.ar: وَلَا يَتَمَنَّوۡنَهُۥٓ أَبَدَۢا بِمَا قَدَّمَتۡ أَيۡدِيهِمۡۚ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمُۢ بِٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
62:7.en: But they will never long for it because of all that their own hands have sent before, and Allah is Aware of evil-doers

62:8.ar: قُلۡ إِنَّ ٱلۡمَوۡتَ ٱلَّذِي تَفِرُّونَ مِنۡهُ فَإِنَّهُۥ مُلَٰقِيكُمۡۖ ثُمَّ تُرَدُّونَ إِلَىٰ عَٰلِمِ ٱلۡغَيۡبِ وَٱلشَّهَٰدَةِ فَيُنَبِّئُكُم بِمَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
62:8.en: Say (unto them, O Muhammad): Lo! the death from which ye shrink will surely meet you, and afterward ye will be returned unto the Knower of the Invisible and the Visible, and He will tell you what ye used to do

cYhGAsGy0io.title: Friday Sermon Workshop, Session 1: Why Jumuah and What a Khutbah Is For
cYhGAsGy0io.one_line: Opening session: public speaking as the engine of change, the sanctity and difficulty of the minbar, what audiences want, and changing one behavior.
cYhGAsGy0io.summary: The first session of his Friday Sermon Workshop lays out the theory behind effective speaking. He argues that public speaking has always been the engine of social change and the one trait effective leaders share, good or bad, and that Muslims own the strongest speaking venue in existence yet waste it. He traces Jumuah back to the pre-Islamic gathering day renamed by the Prophet's ancestor, describes the Prophet's reputation for eloquence and his shift from a soft-spoken private manner to a fiery minbar persona, and insists that every khatib stands in for the Messenger and is held to his standard. Jumuah is the hardest form of speaking: no props, no walking, Arabic requirements, a time limit, and an audience of everyone that Allah gathers for you, though that luck can run out as it did for emptied churches. Audiences want four things: to relate, to connect, answers and solutions. The speaker wants one thing: changed behavior, pursued by focusing on a single measurable behavior, painting a vivid picture of both outcomes, and leading by example. He derives the goals of the khutbah from Surat al-Jumu'ah and closes with the attributes of a successful speaker: knowledge, preparation, articulation, focus, confidence without arrogance, honesty, relevance, observation and piety.

outline.heading: Theory, then trying and failing
outline.gist: He disclaims being a great speaker; what matters is understanding the theory of what makes a good speaker, then trying, failing and trying again until you find your own zone.

outline.heading: Public speaking as the engine of social change
outline.gist: Every major movement in history, civil rights, religious or political, was fuelled by great speakers. Muslims have the most solid speaking venue in the world and still fail to produce the change they hope for.

outline.heading: The one trait effective leaders share
outline.gist: Effective leaders, good or evil, have only public speaking in common: the Prophet and Hitler share nothing else, and even a president with no ethics or plan moved the public from a podium.

outline.heading: From the day of 'Arubah to Jumu'ah
outline.gist: Arabs already gathered on that day in markets to hear poetry and sermons; one of the Prophet's ancestors renamed it Jumu'ah, the gathering, so Islam built on an existing speaking venue.

outline.heading: The Prophet's reputation for eloquence
outline.gist: Even Arabs who died rejecting him knew him for fasahah and khatabah: he could stand anywhere without preparation and speak the high Arabic that only poets and leaders commanded.

outline.heading: Soft-spoken in private, fiery on the minbar
outline.gist: Privately calm, quiet and tender, on the minbar his voice rose and his face reddened as if warning of an army behind the hill, as Jabir describes. Showmanship is fine in its proper context: the minbar calls for a different register.

outline.heading: Standing in for the Messenger
outline.gist: Every minbar is the Messenger's. His own ritual before each khutbah is to remember he is filling in for him and ask what he would think and say about this situation; that sanctity has been forgotten.

outline.heading: Why Jumuah is the hardest form of speaking
outline.gist: Few khutbahs anywhere are memorable because the form is restricted: limited props and slides, no walking around, few gestures, required Arabic verses, a set structure, a time limit and set content.

outline.heading: Speaking to everybody
outline.gist: Public speaking 101 demands a target audience, but the khatib addresses everyone at once; master Jumuah and every other kind of speaking becomes easier.

outline.heading: Jumuah is inseparable from leadership
outline.gist: Wherever two or three Muslims settle, even in a small Alaskan town, they set up a minbar to find each other and keep direction. The Prophet and then the caliphs, some of them weak speakers, gave the khutbah as leaders; sucking leadership out of Jumuah left communities aimless.

outline.heading: Allah gathers them; you only deliver
outline.gist: A dars draws fifty people while Jumuah draws a thousand because Allah obliges them to come; the khatib's job is to offer something worth their time, with understanding, answers and a plan.

outline.heading: The luck can run out
outline.gist: The Prophet warned that what befell the People of the Book will likely befall us: like emptied churches and synagogues, masjids can empty unless people find something meaningful.

outline.heading: They come for Jumuah, not for you
outline.gist: Knowing nobody came to hear him is humbling. Jumuah is obligatory even if the khutbah is in a language you do not understand, and the khutbah is part of the prayer itself, not just a speech.

outline.heading: What the audience wants: four things
outline.gist: Listeners want to relate to the content, connect with the speaker, get answers to their questions and solutions to their problems; leaving with none of the four is a wasted hour.

outline.heading: Relate: live outside the masjid walls
outline.gist: Imams who have lived between the masjid walls for ten years cannot say anything relevant. When he came to Canada he had to discard hundreds of examples and seerah parallels; the first one he tried met total silence.

outline.heading: Connect with the person
outline.gist: Connection is separate from relevance and depends on delivery; you need not reach everyone, only enough people that the rest feel it, and a speaker who connects with no one knows it within minutes.

outline.heading: Answers woven into the talk
outline.gist: Keep an ear to the ground for common questions and insert the answers throughout the talk; stating 'here is the question, here is the answer' kills most of the impact.

outline.heading: Solutions, the hardest of the four
outline.gist: A real solution is almost impossible in a 15 to 20 minute khutbah, but the talk must at least take steps in a direction.

outline.heading: What the speaker wants: changed behavior
outline.gist: Everything else serves one goal, changing people's behavior, including your own. Never speak on trivial topics like water over soda; behavior never changes by accident, only when changing it is the goal, as it was for the Prophet.

outline.heading: Focus on one behavior
outline.gist: Talk about one behavior, not five or six, and keep drilling that one change until you see its effect in people's lives; he admits he still drifts when excited.

outline.heading: Make the change measurable
outline.gist: Give people a valid, tangible way to tell whether the behavior is improving or worsening in their own lives; this is the most often missed point.

outline.heading: Paint a vivid picture of both futures
outline.gist: Describe the problem, what it should look like, and what happens if nothing changes, as the Quran does through its stories. When societies do not change, it is because their speakers have not painted the picture.

outline.heading: Measuring change: ikhlas and anger
outline.gist: Asked what measurable means, he gives ikhlas as a hard case that still has valid measures, and anger as an easy one: how many times a week do I lose my temper.

outline.heading: Lead by example: held to the Prophet's standard
outline.gist: Whoever stands on the Prophet's minbar is judged by his example and can no longer excuse himself like everyone else; if you are not ready, stand behind. The stakes and the reward are both high, and Allah addressed even the Prophet sternly when people's words affected him.

outline.heading: Goal one: recite the signs and explain the creed
outline.gist: Surat al-Jumu'ah sets the khutbah's purposes. First, tell people who Allah is through His signs so they understand their creed and their relationship with Him.

outline.heading: Goal two: purify the hearts
outline.gist: Yuzakkihim: cleanse people's insides and change how they think, which changes how they feel and then how they behave.

outline.heading: Goal three: rulings with wisdom
outline.gist: Teach what is halal and what is not, with the hikmah to know which ruling applies now and which later.

outline.heading: Goal four: raise real awareness
outline.gist: The surah then describes those who carry information without understanding; the khutbah must truly educate and enlighten.

outline.heading: Goal five: action over lineage
outline.gist: Against the claim of being the children of Musa and Ibrahim, stress that only action counts, not background, family or wealth.

outline.heading: Goal six: remind of accountability
outline.gist: The surah ends on accountability. Allah did not leave the khutbah as a vague 'reminder'; its elements are spelled out in the surah named after it.

outline.heading: Course theory, part one: delivery
outline.gist: About six theory sessions before practice, starting with delivery: body language, tone, voice, sitting or standing, moving, gestures and props, which matter more than what is said.

outline.heading: Course theory, part two: content needs a twist
outline.gist: What content suits a Jumuah and other settings; everyone has heard every topic many times, so if you have no twist, pick something else.

outline.heading: Course theory, part three: Jumuah specifics
outline.gist: Jumuah has many specifics, such as dress code: give it in jeans and people will talk about nothing else, so close the holes people can poke at.

outline.heading: Improvising: his teacher's surprise topic
outline.gist: Practice will include prepared talks and improvisation. His teacher, as they pulled up for a condolence visit, told him to speak on the long hadith in Musnad Ahmad about death; he bombed, but learned to structure thoughts fast and later produced poetry on the spot when he had nothing prepared.

outline.heading: Feedback and styles
outline.gist: Learning to take feedback matters; he will speak first and invite them to tear his talk apart, then try different styles and scenarios.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute one: knowledge
outline.gist: Never explain what you do not understand yourself, say 'I don't know' when needed, and build knowledge for life; many khatibs lack knowledge of the world more than of the Sharia. He points to a long Arabic public-speaking series and Stephen Covey.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute two: preparation
outline.gist: Out of respect for any audience he always prepares, even ten minutes for a topic he has given for years or a family gathering.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute three: articulation
outline.gist: Command of English or Arabic, vocabulary and grammar is the first thing people hear; strong articulation can carry a speaker who lacks the other tools.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute four: focus
outline.gist: Stay on one topic from several angles and avoid istitrad, digression, which he confesses is his own habit.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute five: confidence, not arrogance
outline.gist: The line is thin; if you cannot hit confidence, come off shaky rather than arrogant, because people sympathize with the first and reject the second.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute six: honesty and credibility
outline.gist: People sniff out a hypocrite almost immediately; if you do not believe and live what you say, they feel it.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute seven: relevance
outline.gist: Speak to people according to what they know, their age, background and experience.

outline.heading: The village imam who preached love to farmers
outline.gist: A soft-hearted young imam in his Syrian mountain village reached no one with talks on love until, on his advice, he warned of seventy years' fall in Jahannam for denying daughters their inheritance; six rows came to Fajr, and he stayed ten years. Know your audience's nature.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute eight: observation
outline.gist: Read every person every moment and adjust: move on when they are bored, clarify when they are lost. Masks make this hard, forcing him to read eyes alone.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute nine: piety and leading by example
outline.gist: Practise what you preach; you need not be perfect, but never tell people to do what you are not doing yourself.

GBgQ1Xgzk78.title: Friday Sermon Workshop, Session 2: Vocal Delivery
GBgQ1Xgzk78.one_line: Workshop session on using the voice: speed and repetition, vocalizing emotion, clarity, tone, humor and seriousness, slang, and the power of the pause.
GBgQ1Xgzk78.summary: Second session of his Friday Sermon Workshop, the first on delivery. He opens with Mehrabian's 7/38/55 rule: content captures only seven percent of an audience's attention, so deep scholars go unheard while empty performers draw millions of views, and the point of learning showmanship is to let the seven percent of content arrive. He names four bad habits (always high, always low, too loud, too sharp) and then four rules. Speed: slow beats fast, but vary pace to signal what matters, as the Quran does when it tells the same story at different lengths, and repeat key sentences functionally as the Prophet repeated things three times. Emotion: the voice must carry sadness, anger, happiness, mockery, questions and surprise, and sarcasm that is not vocalized clearly backfires. Clarity: enunciate every letter and check pronunciation, especially for an audience whose first language is not English or Arabic. Tone: never stay monotonic more than ten to fifteen seconds, but never exaggerate, because listeners detect anything not genuine. He adds tips: imitate a speaker you admire until you break off into your own style, cut filler ticks, use humor only when it serves the point and never at the start or end, learn to shift into seriousness, use a little slang, and master silence, since public speaking is the art of the pause.

outline.heading: The 7/38/55 rule
outline.gist: In Mehrabian's rule, content earns only 7 percent of an audience's attention, voice 38 and body language 55. Scholars with mind-blowing content go unheard while performers with nothing to say get millions of views.

outline.heading: Bad vocalization one: always high
outline.gist: A voice pitched high the whole time makes people scroll past within seconds, even when the message matters.

outline.heading: Bad vocalization two: always low
outline.gist: Staying deep and low the whole time loses people too; the skill is moving up and down to suit what you emphasize.

outline.heading: Bad vocalization three: too loud
outline.gist: He admits this is his own fault: getting passionate and yelling for seven or eight minutes. Loudness works only for a few moments.

outline.heading: Bad vocalization four: too sharp
outline.gist: A sharp sound, often from microphone distance or volume settings, makes everyone cringe.

outline.heading: His machine-gun speed
outline.gist: Years ago he spoke so fast that older men stopped him mid-talk to make him repeat everything. You learn the rules and improve; what remains becomes your persona.

outline.heading: Rule one, speed: slow beats fast
outline.gist: When in doubt go slower; it costs you 15 to 30 percent of your content and slowing your words slows your thinking, but people understand and enjoy you more.

outline.heading: Speed for emphasis: the Quran's retellings
outline.gist: Jog through the context and slow down at the point. The Quran keeps every element of a story but gives Musa's encounter with Pharaoh fifty verses in one surah and two in another, depending on the point there.

outline.heading: Slow down on the Prophet's words
outline.gist: Narrate the setting of a hadith quickly, then say his words slowly and clearly; otherwise people leave knowing they heard a story but not why.

outline.heading: Repetition: the Prophet's threefold pattern
outline.gist: The Prophet repeated things three times, but never identically; each repetition pushed people to think further. He demonstrates a functional threefold repetition.

outline.heading: Repeat one key sentence
outline.gist: Good speakers choose a sentence that matters and repeat it in different ways through the talk so the audience leaves with it memorized; fast speakers especially need repetition.

outline.heading: Rule two, emotion: sadness
outline.gist: The voice must carry the emotion. For sadness, such as the Prophet weeping over his son Ibrahim, come down, slow and leave space; khatibs who yell while crying are playing on emotion.

outline.heading: Emotion: anger
outline.gist: Anger goes louder, sharper and abrupt, as in the Prophet's rebuke when companions traded racist insults: leave it, it is rotten.

outline.heading: Why khatibs sound angry
outline.gist: The Prophet's minbar persona was loud and seemed angry because he addressed critical matters and wanted people alert and ready for change, not laid back.

outline.heading: Emotion: happiness
outline.gist: Happiness lifts the voice higher.

outline.heading: His mother followed a speaker by his voice alone
outline.gist: His mother could not follow a speaker's dialect yet understood everything from the rise and fall of his voice: good vocalization carries meaning even when the words do not.

outline.heading: Emotion: mockery and sarcasm
outline.gist: Mockery needs its own voice, as when the chiefs taunted Nuh building the ark: you were a prophet, now a carpenter.

outline.heading: When sarcasm backfired
outline.gist: A listener took his sarcastic khutbah line about the cartoons of the Prophet literally and confronted him. Sarcasm says the opposite of the message, so it must sound clearly different from your normal voice, or leave it.

outline.heading: Emotion: questions
outline.gist: Questions rise at the end; scholars even taught that questions in the Quran should be recited as questions, though that is hard to do in prayer.

outline.heading: Emotion: surprise
outline.gist: After building suspense, surprise needs an abrupt change in tone, volume or nature of the voice; done well it can make the whole speech.

outline.heading: Rule three, clarity: enunciation
outline.gist: Clarity matters most for audiences hearing a second language. Every letter must come out, unlike the joke about the man who drops last letters; tajweed is training in exactly this.

outline.heading: Clarity: pronunciation
outline.gist: Say words the way your audience is used to hearing them; Muhammad Hamou listed every word he mispronounced when he arrived. Clear enunciation and pronunciation alone can carry a speaker for years.

outline.heading: Rule four, tone: never monotonic
outline.gist: Monotony is a main reason people sleep in Jumuah. Never hold one tone more than 10 to 15 seconds; ideally the tone moves within every sentence.

outline.heading: Don't exaggerate: stay genuine
outline.gist: Exaggerated tone changes bother him most: people detect anything not genuine and stop listening. Showmanship exists only so the seven percent of content arrives; this is not theater or stand-up comedy.

outline.heading: Imitate a speaker, then break off
outline.gist: Watch speakers you admire for how they deliver, not what they say, and imitate them until you develop your own recipe; every reciter with a good Quran voice imitated someone, and those who did not read dully all their lives.

outline.heading: Drop your filler ticks
outline.gist: Fillers like 'you know' or 'fa-mma' repeated endlessly signal uncertainty. His own is 'yani', even in medical interviews; a sheikh who always said 'na'am' said it in prayer when corrected and confused everyone.

outline.heading: Humor: never open or close with a joke
outline.gist: Humor is the most dangerous tool: a joke that bombs at the start ends the talk, never sell a joke before telling it, and a failed closing joke is the cow kicking over the milk pail.

outline.heading: Humor must be functional
outline.gist: A joke inside the talk must serve the sequence of thought, never be thrown in just to make people laugh.

outline.heading: Topics never to joke about
outline.gist: Disabilities, religions, catastrophes, looks, weight and anything that can sound sexist, especially from a Muslim man; second-wife jokes, most of his own repertoire, are off the table.

outline.heading: Laughter and tears, as with the Prophet
outline.gist: He rarely jokes, but the companions said the Prophet made them laugh and cry; drawing both emotions naturally relaxes people and makes them listen.

outline.heading: Shifting into seriousness
outline.gist: Seriousness does not need a stern face or a sharp voice; it is the shift from a laid-back story to raising the tension in the room, moving back and forth between humor and gravity using speed, emotion and tone.

outline.heading: Attention spans have collapsed
outline.gist: Songs are three minutes and talks online must be under ten to be heard, so speakers need every tool. In his father's youth a village hakawati held everyone with made-up stories because there was nothing else.

outline.heading: In Arabic: fusha with a safe sukun
outline.gist: Speak fusha, and if unsure of a case ending put a sukun on the last letter; back home a wrong vowel on the minbar could end you, and he once saw a khatib corrected mid-khutbah.

outline.heading: A little slang, as the Prophet used Habashi words
outline.gist: In English, a few words a particular group uses win their attention, never profanity. The Prophet learned Habashi words such as 'sanah' and used them with Abyssinian Muslims so they felt included.

outline.heading: The art of the pause
outline.gist: Public speaking is the art of the pause: a few seconds of silence lets people weigh what you said, anticipate what comes, and absorb it. Do not fill every second.

outline.heading: Why the Prophet sat between the two khutbahs
outline.gist: He reads the sitting as a moment for listeners to hear their own thoughts, since they cannot listen to you and to themselves at once.

outline.heading: Pause without looking lost
outline.gist: Too much silence is awkward; even when your mind goes blank, pause so it does not look like forgetting. Stop just before your most important word, and never fill gaps with 'um'.

outline.heading: Get comfortable with silence
outline.gist: Like a therapist at ease in a quiet room, a speaker must be comfortable with silence; we are rarely silent in life. Try telling a story with and without pauses.

outline.heading: Recap: four questions while speaking
outline.gist: Avoid the four bad vocalizations except for deliberate moments, and always know your speed, emotion, clarity and tone. Look up any word you cannot pronounce, as he did for 'hoopoe'; stay diverse with humor, seriousness and slang; use the pause, which he admits he uses too little.

cfZ4NITZTng.title: Friday Sermon Workshop, Session 3: Body Language
cfZ4NITZTng.one_line: Workshop session on body language: hands, facial expressions, eye contact, posture and movement, plus practical remedies for stage fright.
cfZ4NITZTng.summary: Third session of his Friday Sermon Workshop, recorded during the December 2020 lockdown. He restates the 7/38/55 rule: content captures only seven percent of attention, voice about a third and body language the majority, which is why deep scholars go unheard while clowns draw crowds. He then works through four parts of body language. Hands must move, but every gesture should match the meaning and emotion of the words; sudden movements, repeated tics, synchronized robotic motion and finger pointing all break the connection. The face must be lit and unobstructed, and a speaker should smile at least once so people know he is human. Eye contact should last three to four seconds per person and be spontaneous, because looking is how a speaker reads and adjusts to his audience. For posture: stand, face people, never turn your back or side, move in small steps rather than pacing, and do not clutch your own hand. He notes that Jumuah strips away most of these tools, which is why it is the hardest form of speaking. He closes with remedies for stage fright: hold on to something, look just above the last head, use a personal pre-talk routine of dhikr, deep breath and smile, do not cram beforehand, and practise aloud, even to walls or to your own family at home.

outline.heading: Body language carries most of the attention
outline.gist: After last session's voice rules he restates that content earns only seven percent of attention, so deep scholars no one can sit through for five minutes go unheard. Body language, in four parts (hands, face, eyes, posture), carries over sixty percent and must be practised clumsily before it works.

outline.heading: Use your hands, though the Arab khatib held a staff
outline.gist: You cannot speak with arms stuck at your sides. Arabs disliked a khatib who gestured, so he held a pole, stick or sword, not to signal war; done that way, Jumuah takes away 70 to 80 percent of body language, so the other tools must be strong.

outline.heading: Gestures must fit the meaning
outline.gist: Saying a man was fat and tall with mismatched hands confuses people. Hands are the most effective part of body language: mute a good speaker and you can still follow the gist.

outline.heading: Why Jumuah strips gestures away
outline.gist: His own theory: Allah removed these enjoyable but distracting tools from Jumuah so the congregation focuses on the content, which otherwise matters little to listeners.

outline.heading: Describing with the hands
outline.gist: When you describe something or say 'we should open our hearts', a matching hand movement makes the listener relate and connect far more.

outline.heading: Gestures carry emotion
outline.gist: Never state your emotion outright; let it come through. Hands coming together bring intensity, closeness or sadness; opening them signals optimism and happiness; touching the face can show fear.

outline.heading: Make every gesture deliberate
outline.gist: No scratching or idle movement; a thought-out gesture, like a hand to the head when someone sees something startling, makes the feeling land. Practice sessions will check that each gesture fits.

outline.heading: Avoid sudden movements
outline.gist: Nearly every gesture has a context where it works, but a sudden one never does: it spikes adrenaline for no reason and makes people uncomfortable. Replace it with a sudden change in voice or face.

outline.heading: The sheikh who banged the minbar
outline.gist: A sheikh from his youth gave hour-long khutbahs, sent people wanting a short one elsewhere, and banged the minbar to wake dozing old men; the bang threw everyone into fight-or-flight. Never force an emotion on the audience.

outline.heading: Avoid repeated mannerisms and robotic symmetry
outline.gist: No windshield-wiper hand repeated for fifteen minutes, no vocal fillers (use silence instead), and no both hands moving in sync; each hand should move on its own, naturally.

outline.heading: Teachers who drilled fixed gestures
outline.gist: Early public-speaking teachers he heard made students memorize set hand movements, and those students spoke all their lives with gestures that carried no meaning or emotion.

outline.heading: Point with the whole hand, not a finger
outline.gist: The Prophet pointed with his full hand; a finger singles people out and invades their space. The same applies to content: say 'we' and 'I' rather than accusing 'you'.

outline.heading: Keep your face well lit
outline.gist: Facial expression is the most underused part of body language; stand where light falls on your face so people can see your expressions.

outline.heading: Trust your instinct when reading faces
outline.gist: Infants read their mothers' faces instantly and we are all wired for it, but we learn to distrust that instinct. If someone close looks distressed, or your teenager looks like he is lying, he is; deal with it before problems pile up.

outline.heading: Nothing between your face and the audience
outline.gist: No masks, no bank of microphones. The minbar was built because crowds grew so large that those at the back could no longer see the Prophet's face; even the livestream camera bothers him for blocking his view of the brothers.

outline.heading: Smile at least once
outline.gist: However heavy the topic, smile at some point, even with a pause, so people know you are human. The Prophet smiled even in Jumuah despite his serious minbar persona.

outline.heading: Keep the smile appropriate
outline.gist: His unusual sense of humor once had an elderly man demand what was funny; smile only where it fits, and in a joke know which part to smile at or the audience laughs at the wrong time.

outline.heading: Don't block your natural expressions
outline.gist: Disgust, happiness, pain and sadness should show on your face. In a coffee shop your face tells the story naturally; at the front, self-consciousness builds walls, and while some emotions need control, not all should be blocked.

outline.heading: His teacher's single tear
outline.gist: People on the autism spectrum struggle to show emotion. A teacher of his, followed by thousands, told moving stories with no expression at all; in ten years the only sign was one tear while recounting the Prophet's death. Those who struggle must consciously practise.

outline.heading: Eyes: a few seconds per person
outline.gist: Hold each person's gaze three to four seconds; longer makes people uncomfortable and singles them out, like a teacher of his who spoke only to him all class; fixing on the same few people loses the room.

outline.heading: Eye contact is how you read the room
outline.gist: Glancing too quickly means you take in nothing; looking is how you see whether people are engaged and adjust tone, pace, posture or material. Masks force him to read eyes alone.

outline.heading: Spontaneous, not systematic
outline.gist: Sweeping the room in a fixed pattern looks robotic, and people do not connect with robots; move from person to person naturally.

outline.heading: Posture: standing beats sitting
outline.gist: Standing raises attention by about 14 percent. He sits for his own halaqahs out of tiredness, and the Prophet gave most talks sitting, so sitting is acceptable, but Jumuah is given standing and standing is always better.

outline.heading: Never turn your back or side
outline.gist: Turning away cuts the connection like pulling the wifi; only do it when acting out a story. The Prophet never turned just his neck to look at something but turned his whole torso.

outline.heading: Stand straight: his first khutbah at a Syrian army camp
outline.gist: At a compulsory summer camp where prayer was banned, a friend pushed him up unprepared to give Jumuah; his left leg drummed audibly, so he leaned on a concrete beam at 45 degrees. Stand straight with no crossed legs or stretching, but if you are shaking, hold something.

outline.heading: Move in a step and half step, never pace
outline.gist: Moving beats standing still, but walking back and forth is useless and unsettling, like a sudden movement. Take a step, then a half step, within a small radius; Jumuah removes this tool too.

outline.heading: Don't hold your hand like it's broken
outline.gist: Clasping one arm as if it needs a cast looks bad; if you are not gesturing, let your hands rest naturally, since a held hand is a tool not being used.

outline.heading: Glossophobia: nerves are normal
outline.gist: Fear of public speaking is the most common phobia; some studies say three quarters of people would rather die than speak. He finds it lower in Canada, where schools train students, than in Syria. A teenager with no nerves at all is the worrying case.

outline.heading: Shaking and sweating are fine
outline.gist: If you shake, hold a chair or anything until you calm down after a few minutes. Sweat as much as you like, but dress so it does not show; baggy clothes help.

outline.heading: Look just above the last head
outline.gist: His trick for four years: look half a metre above the last person and move every two or three seconds. A congregant once felt there was 'some dude behind me'. It costs you the connection and the reading of the room, so use it only until you settle.

outline.heading: Faces are your feedback: this is a service
outline.gist: When someone keeps looking away, something did not work for them; you can figure it out yourself and fix it next time. Speaking is a service, and if it is not helping you sit down or change it.

outline.heading: His routine: dhikr, a deep breath, a smile
outline.gist: Before speaking, say your own adhkar, close your eyes, take a deep breath, smile, then stand up and be yourself; public speaking will change your character over time.

outline.heading: Compensate for what you cannot fix
outline.gist: He once had several people slow him down live until they were satisfied, and at that speed he could no longer think or produce. Know your weakness and make up for it with other strengths, as speakers who cannot stand do.

outline.heading: Imagine something funny
outline.gist: For the very nervous, especially the young: picture the audience with potato heads; laughing inside relaxes you.

outline.heading: Don't review right before
outline.gist: Give whatever you have; for his first six years he delivered under a quarter of what he prepared, and forgetting points will always happen.

outline.heading: Use the bathroom first
outline.gist: Always go before standing in front of people, or your body language will not be the kind you want.

outline.heading: A camera is no audience
outline.gist: Speaking to a camera sucks the life out of public speaking: no engagement, no connection, no faces to feel emotion with.

outline.heading: Give your khutbah to trees and walls
outline.gist: His teacher told him to speak to trees and walls when there was no one; three times he gave a full halaqah in an empty masjid because he had prepared it, and the caretaker who found him stayed to listen.

outline.heading: Hear yourself and find your balance
outline.gist: Only by speaking aloud do you hear what you dislike and change it. Standing up changes your body's chemistry, so the aim is to bring your natural one-on-one self to the front; some must peel off filters and others tone down overexpression.

outline.heading: Give Jumuah to your family at home
outline.gist: Use the lockdown to hold Jumuah at home and let your son, daughter or wife give it, since the rulings are more flexible at home; if your own children will listen to you, you do not need him.

outline.heading: The rules apply to all speaking but performance
outline.gist: Asked where these rules apply: everywhere except theater, stand-up and musical performance, which have their own laws, always adjusted to context.

43:9.ar: وَلَئِن سَأَلۡتَهُم مَّنۡ خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضَ لَيَقُولُنَّ خَلَقَهُنَّ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ
43:9.en: And if thou (Muhammad) ask them: Who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely answer: The Mighty, the Knower created them

43:10.ar: ٱلَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ مَهۡدࣰ ا وَجَعَلَ لَكُمۡ فِيهَا سُبُلࣰ ا لَّعَلَّكُمۡ تَهۡتَدُونَ
43:10.en: Who made the earth a resting-place for you, and placed roads for you therein, that haply ye may find your way

43:11.ar: وَٱلَّذِي نَزَّلَ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ مَآءَۢ بِقَدَرࣲ فَأَنشَرۡنَا بِهِۦ بَلۡدَةࣰ مَّيۡتࣰ اۚ كَذَٰلِكَ تُخۡرَجُونَ
43:11.en: And Who sendeth down water from the sky in (due) measure, and We revive a dead land therewith. Even so will ye be brought forth

43:12.ar: وَٱلَّذِي خَلَقَ ٱلۡأَزۡوَٰجَ كُلَّهَا وَجَعَلَ لَكُم مِّنَ ٱلۡفُلۡكِ وَٱلۡأَنۡعَٰمِ مَا تَرۡكَبُونَ
43:12.en: He Who created all the pairs, and appointed for you ships and cattle whereupon ye ride

43:13.ar: لِتَسۡتَوُۥاْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِۦ ثُمَّ تَذۡكُرُواْ نِعۡمَةَ رَبِّكُمۡ إِذَا ٱسۡتَوَيۡتُمۡ عَلَيۡهِ وَتَقُولُواْ سُبۡحَٰنَ ٱلَّذِي سَخَّرَ لَنَا هَٰذَا وَمَا كُنَّا لَهُۥ مُقۡرِنِينَ
43:13.en: That ye may mount upon their backs, and may remember your Lord's favour when ye mount thereon, and may say: Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us, and we were not capable (of subduing them)

43:14.en: And lo! unto our Lord we surely are returning

43:15.ar: وَجَعَلُواْ لَهُۥ مِنۡ عِبَادِهِۦ جُزۡءًاۚ إِنَّ ٱلۡإِنسَٰنَ لَكَفُورࣱ مُّبِينٌ
43:15.en: And they allot to Him a portion of His bondmen! Lo! man is verily a mere ingrate

43:16.ar: أَمِ ٱتَّخَذَ مِمَّا يَخۡلُقُ بَنَاتࣲ وَأَصۡفَىٰكُم بِٱلۡبَنِينَ
43:16.en: Or chooseth He daughters of all that He hath created, and honoureth He you with sons

43:17.ar: وَإِذَا بُشِّرَ أَحَدُهُم بِمَا ضَرَبَ لِلرَّحۡمَٰنِ مَثَلࣰ ا ظَلَّ وَجۡهُهُۥ مُسۡوَدࣰّ ا وَهُوَ كَظِيمٌ
43:17.en: And if one of them hath tidings of that which he likeneth to the Beneficent One, his countenance becometh black and he is full of inward rage

obivBjObti0.title: Az-Zukhruf, Verses 11-19 (Fajr Dars)
obivBjObti0.one_line: Two levels of reflecting on creation, ascribing offspring to Allah as ego and ingratitude, and the pagan logic that valued sons over daughters by money.
obivBjObti0.summary: Continuing Az-Zukhruf, which warns those carrying the message against a materialistic logic that values only what glitters, he explains verses 11-19. The verses on pairs, ships and livestock tell people nothing they did not already know: the Quran is not a science book, and the hunt for scientific miracles reflects a sense of weakness. The verses ask for a second level of reflection beyond how things work: why life wants to live, why the most accessible material happens to float. A Muslim holds both levels, which is why Muslim civilization paired religious rule with flourishing science and why a scholar once meant someone learned in the worldly sciences too. The travel dua should be said with real appreciation that Allah subjected what we could never overpower. Ascribing a son or partner to Allah is the ego's attempt to bring Him down to human size, since we cannot imagine anything beyond time and space, and it is kufr in its sense of supreme ingratitude. The pagan Arabs gave Allah daughters while despising their own, because they measured children by financial value. He contrasts the Prophet's honour of Fatima, notes that Muslims still chase sons and have pushed women out of the masjid, and asks people to stop judging colleagues, businesses and masajid by output and money alone.

outline.heading: Az-Zukhruf: the first warning in the Ha-Mim cluster
outline.gist: The Ha-Mim surahs advise those who carry the message; this one warns against a materialistic logic that gives value to what looks shiny but has no substance.

outline.heading: Admitting Allah created, yet wanting a god you can touch
outline.gist: They say Allah created everything yet worship stone, because they need something tangible; humanity has tried worshipping almost everything and it never works. He recalls the earth spread out with pathways and recites the next verses.

outline.heading: Pairs, ships and livestock: nothing they did not know
outline.gist: The creation verses only point to what people already see; their job is to turn attention toward contemplating where these things came from.

outline.heading: The hunt for scientific miracles
outline.gist: Searching the Quran for discoveries reflects a collective feeling of weakness; revelation and the world share one source so they never contradict, but that is not the book's purpose.

outline.heading: Two levels of reflection
outline.gist: Science asks how things happen and yields energy and cures; the Muslim adds a higher level that asks why it all exists and whether it has a purpose.

outline.heading: Why does life want to live?
outline.gist: His question to young people drawn to atheism: who programmed the first cell with the will to survive? Science does not fail to answer it, it simply does not care to ask.

outline.heading: Why does the nearest material float?
outline.gist: Science explains buoyancy and builds great ships, but why is wood, the easiest thing to reach, the thing that floats and saves you from drowning?

outline.heading: Settle on their backs, then remember the favour
outline.gist: The verse moves from using creation to recognising the blessing behind it; it is not one level or the other but fully both, benefiting from creation and improving it.

outline.heading: We could never overpower what carries us
outline.gist: Humans are physically among the weakest creatures; our edge is cognitive, the companions were far stronger than us, and he calls himself a medical miracle. Advancement was possible only because Allah made resources accessible.

outline.heading: Glory to Him who subjected this to us
outline.gist: Muslims were never asked to neglect science; Allah keeps pointing to creation so we learn from it and improve.

outline.heading: A religious civilization that backed science
outline.gist: He knows of no other era when a religious regime championed science; Muslim scholars were also botanists, geologists and astronomers.

outline.heading: What the word scholar used to mean
outline.gist: Students learned religion in the masjid and a profession for a livelihood; an alim meant someone learned in worldly sciences as well, not someone left poor on a board's payroll.

outline.heading: Do not let the travel dua become habit
outline.gist: A purely material view thanks the carmaker; the believer pauses to appreciate that what carries him was made subservient to him.

outline.heading: Assigning Him a portion of His servants
outline.gist: Claims of a wife, a son or divided entities try to bring the Creator to the level of His creation.

outline.heading: We cannot imagine beyond time and space
outline.gist: Everything we can picture is bound by time and space and is therefore something Allah could create; He is First and Last and Apparent and Hidden, beyond both limits.

outline.heading: The ego resents an all-powerful God
outline.gist: The ego either wants to become more than human, hence superheroes, or to break God down by giving Him a wife and child so He seems relatable.

outline.heading: Kufr as the highest ingratitude
outline.gist: Man is clearly ungrateful: kufr at root means ingratitude, and refusing to credit the Giver of life for the gift of conscious existence is its highest degree.

outline.heading: Daughters for Allah, sons for themselves
outline.gist: Besides giving Him offspring, they chose daughters for Him because they themselves valued sons for the financial strength they brought the tribe.

outline.heading: A face darkened by news of a daughter
outline.gist: Told of the very thing they assigned to Allah, they sat suppressing their anger, and some buried infant girls alive; the verses go after a logic that sees only financial value.

outline.heading: Three daughters and Jannah
outline.gist: Their narrow, one-dimensional thinking made the pre-Islamic period extreme, which is why the Prophet repeatedly promised Jannah for raising daughters well.

outline.heading: The Prophet and Fatima
outline.gist: He loved no one more than his daughter; when she entered he stood, kissed her and seated her in his place, a sunnah for every parent of daughters.

outline.heading: Tawhid was not their real objection
outline.gist: Idols at the Kaaba were prestige and alliance contracts between tribes; what Quraysh resisted most were social changes like these.

outline.heading: Raised in ornaments, weak in argument
outline.gist: Their stated reason for not wanting daughters: they cost money for jewellery and cannot defend the tribe in a fight, a one-dimensional material metric.

outline.heading: His legacy through his daughters
outline.gist: The devaluing was always greed; the Prophet's three sons died in infancy and his lineage continues through Fatima, which is what Allah chose for him.

outline.heading: Muslims still chase a son
outline.gist: Fourteen centuries later families keep having children until a boy arrives, while few keep going for a daughter, a sign the lesson has not landed.

outline.heading: Angels made female
outline.gist: Calling the angels female is another way to weaken the image of Allah; were they witnesses to their creation? Their claim will be recorded and questioned.

outline.heading: Women pushed out of the masjid
outline.gist: The surah opens with the hardest example, valuing women; the Prophet's masjid was about sixty to forty men to women, while today it is eighty to twenty because women were made to feel unwelcome.

outline.heading: Every lesson here applies directly
outline.gist: He asks people to find every example of materialistic logic the surah gives, because unlike many surahs its lessons need no parallels to reach us.

outline.heading: Measuring people by output alone
outline.gist: Performance metrics are easy to build, but trustworthiness, love and empathy go unmeasured though they matter more; at work you care whether a colleague understands you, and employers should keep that balance.

outline.heading: Success measured only in money
outline.gist: Productive people who abuse authority are tolerated and competition turns vicious when money is the only measure; he asks whether masajid can be assessed that way too.

llv7LBBlMeA.title: Az-Zukhruf, Verses 1-10 (Fajr Dars)
llv7LBBlMeA.one_line: Opening Az-Zukhruf: a warning against materialistic logic, from defining success by money to idolizing people, with foreknowledge and the unseen explained.
llv7LBBlMeA.summary: He chooses Az-Zukhruf because, within the Ha-Mim cluster that advises those carrying the message, it is the first to warn: zukhruf is decoration that glitters but has no real value, and the surah dismantles a materialistic logic that no Muslim can live by. No generation has faced more consumerism; even children now define success by money or fame, when it was always service, relationships, peace of heart and reputation. Explaining verses 1-10, he says the Quran is Arabic because its first audience was Arab, and that the Mother of the Book is Allah's knowledge alone. Knowing the future does not mean Allah programmed us; assuming so equates His knowledge with ours. Belief requires accepting an unseen that cannot be measured, and a Muslim must avoid both superstition and materialism, the greater risk today. Allah does not withhold the reminder from an extravagant people; the emptiness inside cannot be filled with possessions, and research confirms happiness comes from relationships, which is what Allah offers. Prophets were always mocked for material things, and nations that valued everything by money turned savage, as hunger and neglected diseases of the poor show. Finally, people who admit Allah created everything still wanted a tangible idol; today that idol is often a leader we refuse to see as flawed.

outline.heading: The Ha-Mim cluster: advice for carriers of the message
outline.gist: Each surah gives one piece of advice for those serving the deen: dua and connection with Allah, calling through conduct rather than words, good company and consultation.

outline.heading: Zukhruf: glitter with no substance
outline.gist: The first in the cluster to warn; zukhruf is decoration you throw away after the occasion, unlike gold which has real value. The surah attacks the logic of materialistic value from many angles.

outline.heading: An age of unprecedented consumerism
outline.gist: He doubts any era has pushed people so forcefully toward seeing everything materially, which makes the surah fitting for Ramadan.

outline.heading: Success without money or fame
outline.gist: Neither wealth nor fame was ever needed for success, yet it is now hard to imagine success without them and children grow up defining it that way.

outline.heading: Then what is success?
outline.gist: A young listener once asked him exactly that; the answer is service, relationships, peace of heart and a good reputation. He urges reading the surah with this in mind, including its distinctive telling of Musa's story.

outline.heading: A late Makkan surah
outline.gist: Surahs fall into early and late Makkan and Madani phases; Az-Zukhruf came around the sixtieth in order, in the last three or four years in Makkah. Every Ha-Mim surah shares a common background.

outline.heading: By the clear, clarifying book
outline.gist: Mubin can mean clear in itself or clarifying for others; both apply.

outline.heading: Why an Arabic Quran
outline.gist: It had to come in some language and its first audience was Arab; there is no universal tongue that was passed over. The aim is that you understand.

outline.heading: The Mother of the Book: knowledge only Allah holds
outline.gist: Scholars differ on what exactly it is, but such phrases refer to the knowledge beyond the book we read that no creature can access.

outline.heading: If it is written, why act?
outline.gist: Young people keep asking this about destiny; it only means the future is known to Allah and to no one else.

outline.heading: Foreknowledge without programming
outline.gist: We can only predict what has no choice, like a car aimed at a wall or code before pressing enter; assuming Allah knows the same way equates our knowledge with His. He knows though we are not programmed, because He is Allah.

outline.heading: Stop comparing Allah to yourself
outline.gist: The urge to assume He works as we do is human arrogance; nothing is like Him. The Quran is then described as exalted and wise.

outline.heading: Exalted and wise: what cannot be measured
outline.gist: The surah opens by pointing to what is not tangible or observable, which materialistic logic does not even allow, while Islam requires critical thinking and never blind following.

outline.heading: Belief in Allah means accepting an unseen
outline.gist: You cannot believe in a deity and expect nothing to be beyond your knowledge; Allah describes Himself as knower of the unseen and the seen.

outline.heading: The unseen can slide into superstition
outline.gist: Not knowing how to deal with realms like the jinn leads some people to abandon critical thinking.

outline.heading: Keep the pendulum in the middle
outline.gist: Denying the unseen and abandoning worldly planning in the name of destiny are both wrong; today the far greater risk is materialism.

outline.heading: Shall We turn the reminder away from you?
outline.gist: An Arabic figure of speech for looking the other way: should the Quran be withheld because you are an extravagant people? The answer is no.

outline.heading: Israf: the extravagant mindset
outline.gist: Valuing wealth beyond its worth, spending more than you have and misusing what Allah gave, a challenge he recently addressed in another talk.

outline.heading: An emptiness possessions cannot fill
outline.gist: The musrif keeps acquiring, but houses, cars and cottages only make the inner emptiness grow hungrier.

outline.heading: Only dust fills the son of Adam
outline.gist: At death you see that all the money in the world was not worth an hour with a parent, sibling or child, nor a day estranged from a relative; we are soil that enjoyed soil, and only love and connection remain.

outline.heading: What the happiness research found
outline.gist: A long Harvard study found happy people had strong marriages, family ties and social networks, not higher income; beyond roughly seventy to eighty thousand dollars more money adds nothing.

outline.heading: What Allah offers is a relationship
outline.gist: Waking up after reaching six figures changes nothing; salah is not a checkbox but a relationship being built, and that is what brings happiness.

outline.heading: Prophets mocked for material things
outline.gist: Trace mockery through the Quran: it always comes from disbelievers and always targets poverty, weakness, youth or difference, never depth or wisdom.

outline.heading: Destroying those mightier in savagery
outline.gist: Batsh is indiscriminate destruction that spares no child, woman, civilian or tree; Allah destroyed nations more savage than Quraysh.

outline.heading: When everything is valued by the dollar
outline.gist: Nations given much become powerful and then savage; when worth is only money the world's balance breaks and people starve amid plenty.

outline.heading: Diseases of the poor go unresearched
outline.gist: From medicine he notes illnesses affecting only poor populations see little research while others attract a flood of new drugs, for an ugly reason.

outline.heading: The Almighty, the All-Knowing
outline.gist: Asked who created everything, they say Allah; the two names come together to correct the idea that a God beyond reach might not know what is happening.

outline.heading: Then what is Hubal for?
outline.gist: Admitting a Creator beyond time and space yet keeping idols is broken materialistic logic: people want something they can hold, see and speak to.

outline.heading: Today's idol is a human being
outline.gist: If the materialistic mindset remains, removing the stone idol just brings a substitute: scholars, leaders, even a Pharaoh; he sees an inability to accept people as people.

outline.heading: Follow leaders who are flawed
outline.gist: The need for leaders and speakers to be perfect super-people is dangerous; the Prophet never taught it, and Muslims have always benefited from flawed people's skill and wisdom.

outline.heading: The earth spread out like a cradle
outline.gist: Allah made the globe flat for walking, a bed you are born into and return to, with roads to explore.

outline.heading: Roads on earth, guidance of the soul
outline.gist: The verse links physical paths to spiritual guidance, a connection the whole surah keeps making: the material world is a sign of something far bigger.
